column9: Which subatomic particle has a positive charge?
column16: Electron
column28: Protons (p⁺) are positive. Neutrons (n⁰) have no charge, and electrons (e⁻) and the electron cloud they make up are negative.
column29: Think of the particle symbols: p⁺, n⁰, e⁻. Which one has the plus sign?

column9: Where is almost all of an atom's mass located?
column16: In the nucleus
column28: The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons, which are 1 amu each, so it holds the mass. Electrons are about 0 amu, so the electron cloud holds the volume, not the mass.
column29: Which particles are 1 amu each, and where do they live?

column9: Protons and neutrons are made of quarks, but electrons are not.
column28: True. Quarks are the smallest known particles that make up protons and neutrons. Electrons are not made of quarks (a common mistake is thinking all three particles are).
column29: Quarks build the particles that live in one specific place in the atom. Which place?

column9: The ___ number is the number of protons in an atom, and it identifies the element.
column28: The atomic number = number of protons. It identifies the element, and the periodic table is arranged by it.
column29: It is the whole number printed in each box of the periodic table.

column9: Match each particle to its description.
column14: Proton :: Positive charge, found in the nucleus
column15: Neutron :: No charge, found in the nucleus
column16: Electron :: Negative charge, found in the electron cloud
column17: Quark :: Smallest known particle that makes up protons and neutrons
column28: Proton: positive, in the nucleus, 1 amu. Neutron: no charge, in the nucleus, 1 amu. Electron: negative, in the electron cloud, 0 amu. Quarks are the smallest known particles that make up protons and neutrons.
column29: Start with the charges: p⁺, n⁰, e⁻. Then ask which one lives outside the nucleus.

column9: Which symbol represents a neutron?
column16: N
column28: n⁰ is the neutron: n for neutron and 0 for no charge. p⁺ is a proton, e⁻ is an electron, and N is the symbol for the element nitrogen.
column29: The little superscript shows the charge. Which particle has zero charge?

column9: Using our class rule for particle masses, what is the mass of one neutron? Answer in amu.
column28: A neutron has a mass of 1 amu, the same as a proton. An electron is about 0 amu.
column29: Our rule: protons and neutrons are the "heavy" particles. How many amu is "heavy"?

column9: The mass number of an element is printed in its box on the periodic table.
column28: False. The mass number (protons + neutrons) is NOT on the periodic table. The decimal number in the box is the average atomic mass; you round it to get the mass number of the most common isotope.
column29: Look at the decimal number in a periodic table box. Is a count of particles ever a decimal?

column9: A neutral atom has an atomic number of 10. How many electrons does it have?
column28: In a neutral atom, # e⁻ = # p⁺ = atomic number, so it has 10 electrons.
column29: In a neutral atom, which particle count matches the number of electrons?

column9: In a neutral atom, which two numbers are always equal?
column16: Neutrons and electrons
column28: Electrically neutral means the same number of (+) protons and (−) electrons, so the charges cancel to 0. Neutrons often differ from protons.
column29: Neutral means the overall charge is 0. Which two particles have opposite charges?

column9: The space around the nucleus where the electrons are found is called the electron ___.
column28: The electron cloud surrounds the nucleus and is divided into shells (energy levels). It holds the volume of the atom.
column29: It is a weather word that describes something big, fuzzy, and spread out.

column9: Who am I? "I have no charge, but I still add 1 amu to the atom's mass. I live in the nucleus with the protons."
column16: Quark
column28: The neutron (n⁰) has no charge, has a mass of 1 amu, and is in the nucleus. The proton is also in the nucleus but is positive.
column29: Which particle's symbol has a 0 on it?

column9: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom? Select all that apply.
column16: Neutrons
column28: The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons. Electrons, including valence electrons, are in the electron cloud around the nucleus.
column29: The nucleus is the dense center that holds the mass. Which particles are 1 amu?

column9: For our purposes, what is the greatest number of electrons the first shell (closest to the nucleus) can hold?
column28: Shells fill 2, 8, 8 for our purposes, so the first shell holds at most 2 electrons.
column29: Remember the shell pattern we use: __, 8, 8.

column9: Electrons in shells farther from the nucleus have less energy than electrons close to the nucleus.
column28: False. Electrons farther from the nucleus have MORE energy. The outermost (valence) electrons have the most energy.
column29: Shells are also called energy levels. Do the outer electrons have more or less energy?

column9: An atom has an atomic number of 16 and a mass number of 34. How many neutrons does it have?
column28: n⁰ = mass # − atomic # = 34 − 16 = 18 neutrons.
column29: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

column9: Iron (Fe) has atomic number 26 and an average atomic mass of 55.845. How many neutrons are in an atom of the most common isotope of iron?
column28: Round the average atomic mass to get the mass number: 55.845 → 56. n⁰ = 56 − 26 = 30 neutrons.
column29: No mass number given? Round the average atomic mass first, then use mass number − atomic number.

column9: Rubidium (Rb) has atomic number 37 and an average atomic mass of 85.468. How many neutrons are in an atom of the most common isotope of rubidium?
column28: Mass number = 85.468 rounded = 85. n⁰ = 85 − 37 = 48 neutrons.
column29: Round the average atomic mass to a whole number, then use mass number − atomic number.

column9: An atom has 9 protons, 10 neutrons, and 9 electrons. What is its mass number?
column28: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 9 + 10 = 19. Electrons are about 0 amu, so they are not counted (19 + 9 = 28 is the common mistake).
column29: Mass number counts only the particles that have a mass of 1 amu.

column9: Potassium-39 is written $^{39}_{19}\text{K}$. How many neutrons does one atom of potassium-39 have?
column28: Top number = mass number (39), bottom number = atomic number (19). n⁰ = 39 − 19 = 20 neutrons.
column29: The top number is the mass number and the bottom number is the atomic number. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

column9: Calcium has atomic number 20. How many neutrons are in one atom of calcium-44?
column28: In hyphen notation the number after the name is the mass number. n⁰ = 44 − 20 = 24 neutrons.
column29: The number after the hyphen is the mass number. Then use mass number − atomic number.

column9: Nitrogen (N) has atomic number 7 and an average atomic mass of 14.007. How many total subatomic particles (protons + neutrons + electrons) are in a neutral atom of the most common isotope of nitrogen?
column28: Mass number = 14. p⁺ = 7, n⁰ = 14 − 7 = 7, e⁻ = 7 (neutral). Total = 7 + 7 + 7 = 21.
column29: Find p⁺, n⁰, and e⁻ separately, then add all three. Neutral means e⁻ = p⁺.

column9: Which is the correct electron arrangement for a neutral magnesium atom (atomic number 12)?
column28: 12 electrons fill from the inside out: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, and the last 2 in the third: 2-8-2. The second shell can't hold 10, and the order goes inside out.
column29: Fill from the inside out: the first shell holds 2, the second holds 8.

column9: Oxygen has atomic number 8. Write the electron arrangement of a neutral oxygen atom like this example: 2-8-1. Answer: ___
column28: 8 electrons: 2 fill the first shell, and the other 6 go in the second shell, so 2-6.
column29: How many electrons does a neutral atom with 8 protons have? Fill the first shell (2) before the second.

column9: Silicon has atomic number 14. How many electrons are in the outermost shell of a neutral silicon atom?
column28: 14 electrons fill 2, then 8, then the rest: 2-8-4. The outermost (third) shell has 4 electrons.
column29: Fill shells from the inside out using 2, 8, 8 until you run out of electrons.

column9: Potassium has atomic number 19. How many shells (energy levels) hold electrons in a neutral potassium atom?
column28: 19 electrons fill 2-8-8, and the last 1 starts a new shell: 2-8-8-1. That is 4 shells (and potassium is in period 4).
column29: Fill 2, 8, 8, then see if any electrons are left over for another shell.

column9: An atom has 15 protons, 16 neutrons, and 15 electrons. Which element is it?
column16: Phosphorus (atomic number 15)
column28: The number of protons identifies the element: 15 protons = atomic number 15 = phosphorus. Sulfur matches the neutrons and gallium matches the mass number (15 + 16 = 31), which are common mix-ups.
column29: Only one particle count identifies the element. Which one?

column9: A neutral atom has 12 electrons and 13 neutrons. Which element is it?
column16: Carbon (atomic number 6)
column28: Neutral means e⁻ = p⁺, so it has 12 protons. Atomic number 12 = magnesium. Aluminum matches the neutrons and manganese matches the mass number (12 + 13 = 25).
column29: In a neutral atom, the electrons tell you the protons. Then match the protons to the atomic number.

column9: Boron's box on the periodic table shows 10.81. Which statement best explains why 10.81 is NOT boron's mass number?
column14: The mass number is a whole-number count of protons + neutrons in one atom; 10.81 is the average mass of all of boron's isotopes.
column15: 10.81 includes the mass of boron's electrons, so you must subtract them to get the mass number.
column16: The mass number is always smaller than the atomic number, and 10.81 is too big.
column17: Each neutron in boron weighs 0.81 amu, so the decimal comes from the neutrons.
column28: Mass number = protons + neutrons in one atom, always a whole number, and it is not on the periodic table. The average atomic mass is a weighted average of all the isotopes; rounding it (10.81 → 11) gives the mass number of the most common isotope.
column29: Can you have 0.81 of a proton or a neutron? What does the decimal number on the table average together?

column9: If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a marble on the 50-yard line. What does this model show?
column14: The nucleus holds most of the volume, and the electron cloud holds most of the mass.
column15: The nucleus holds most of the mass, and the electron cloud holds most of the volume.
column16: The nucleus and the electron cloud hold equal amounts of mass.
column17: The electrons are packed tightly into the center of the atom.
column28: The tiny nucleus (the marble) holds the protons and neutrons, so it has the mass. The electron cloud (the rest of the stadium) takes up almost all of the space, so it has the volume.
column29: Which part is tiny but holds the heavy particles? Which part takes up the space?

column9: Which force holds the electrons in an atom so they don't fly away from the nucleus?
column16: Attraction between the positive nucleus and the negative electron cloud
column28: Opposite charges attract. The (+) nucleus and the (−) electron cloud pull on each other like the north and south ends of two magnets, and that holds the atom together.
column29: Opposite charges attract; like charges repel. Which pair here has opposite charges?

column9: Jae says, "Electrons are like strangers in an elevator: they spread out as far from each other as they can." Which force is Jae describing?
column14: Repulsion between electrons, which gives the electron cloud its volume
column15: Attraction between protons and electrons, which holds the atom together
column16: Repulsion between protons, which takes huge energy to overcome in the nucleus
column17: Attraction between neutrons and electrons, which balances the charges
column28: Like charges repel, so the (−) electrons push away from each other and spread out. That repulsion is what gives the electron cloud its volume.
column29: Strangers spread out because they push away from each other. Which particles push on each other here?

column9: Match each term to what it tells you.
column14: Atomic number :: Number of protons; identifies the element
column15: Mass number :: Number of protons + neutrons
column16: Average atomic mass :: Weighted average of all isotopes; the decimal on the periodic table
column17: Valence electrons :: Electrons in the outermost energy level
column28: Atomic number = protons (identifies the element). Mass number = protons + neutrons (not on the table). Average atomic mass = weighted average of all isotopes (the decimal on the table). Valence electrons = e⁻ in the outermost energy level.
column29: Which one is a decimal on the table? Which one adds two particle counts?

column9: Put the steps for drawing the electrons of a Bohr model in order.
column14: Fill in electrons from the inside out (2, 8, 8)
column15: Find the number of protons from the atomic number
column16: Check that the number of valence electrons matches the group number
column17: In a neutral atom, electrons = protons
column28: 1) p⁺ = atomic #. 2) In a neutral atom, e⁻ = p⁺. 3) Fill the electrons from the inside out (2, 8, 8). 4) Check that the valence electrons match the group #. Each step needs the one before it.
column29: You cannot place electrons until you know how many there are, and the last step is a check.

column9: A neutral atom of fluorine-19 has atomic number 9. Which statements about it are true? Select all that apply.
column16: It has 9 electrons
column28: p⁺ = 9 (atomic #), n⁰ = 19 − 9 = 10, e⁻ = 9 (neutral). 9 electrons fill 2 then 7: 2-7. The mass number is 19, not 9, and there are 9 electrons, not 19.
column29: Find p⁺, n⁰ (mass number − atomic number), and e⁻ first, then fill the shells 2, 8.

column9: An atom has a mass number of 40 and 21 neutrons. Which element is it?
column16: Calcium (atomic number 20)
column28: Atomic number = mass # − neutrons = 40 − 21 = 19, which is potassium. Scandium matches the neutrons and zirconium matches the mass number, the two classic mix-ups.
column29: Rearrange: neutrons = mass number − atomic number, so atomic number = ?

column9: A neutral atom has a mass number of 52 and 28 neutrons. How many electrons does it have?
column28: p⁺ = 52 − 28 = 24. Neutral means e⁻ = p⁺, so it has 24 electrons (this is chromium).
column29: First find the protons from the mass number and neutrons. Then, in a neutral atom, what equals the protons?

column9: Compare carbon-14, $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$, and nitrogen-14, $^{14}_{7}\text{N}$. How many more neutrons does one atom of carbon-14 have than one atom of nitrogen-14?
column28: Carbon-14: 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons. Nitrogen-14: 14 − 7 = 7 neutrons. Difference = 8 − 7 = 1.
column29: Same mass number does not mean same neutrons. Use mass number − atomic number for each atom, then subtract.

column9: Atom A has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. Atom B has 12 protons and 11 neutrons. Which statement is correct?
column14: They are the same element because they have the same mass number.
column15: They have the same mass number, but they are different elements.
column16: They are the same element because they have the same total number of particles in the nucleus.
column17: Atom B is heavier because it has more protons.
column28: Both mass numbers are 23 (11 + 12 and 12 + 11), but A has 11 protons (sodium) and B has 12 protons (magnesium). Only the proton count identifies the element.
column29: Find each mass number, then ask: which particle count decides what element an atom is?

column9: Maya filled in a chart for neutral atoms. Which rows contain a mistake? Select all that apply.
column14: Na: atomic # 11, mass # 23, 11 p⁺, 12 n⁰, 11 e⁻
column15: O: atomic # 8, mass # 16, 8 p⁺, 8 n⁰, 8 e⁻
column16: Mg: atomic # 12, mass # 24, 12 p⁺, 12 n⁰, 24 e⁻
column17: Be: atomic # 4, mass # 9, 4 p⁺, 4 n⁰, 4 e⁻
column18: Li: atomic # 3, mass # 7, 3 p⁺, 4 n⁰, 3 e⁻
column19: C: atomic # 6, mass # 12, 6 p⁺, 6 n⁰, 6 e⁻
column28: Check each row: p⁺ = atomic #, n⁰ = mass # − atomic #, e⁻ = p⁺. Mg should have 12 electrons, not 24 (that is the mass number). Be should have 9 − 4 = 5 neutrons, not 4. The other rows check out.
column29: For each row, test three rules: p⁺ = atomic #, n⁰ = mass number − atomic number, e⁻ = p⁺.

column9: Jae says an atom with 7 protons, 8 neutrons, and 7 electrons has a mass number of 22, because you add all three particles. Which response is best?
column14: Jae is right: every particle in the atom counts toward the mass number.
column15: Jae is wrong: the mass number is the protons only, so it is 7.
column16: Jae is wrong: the mass number is the neutrons minus the protons, so it is 1.
column17: Jae is wrong: electrons are about 0 amu, so the mass number is 7 + 8 = 15.
column28: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 7 + 8 = 15. Electrons are about 0 amu, so adding them (22) is the common mistake.
column29: Which particles have a mass of 1 amu, and which is about 0 amu?

column9: Who am I? "I am a neutral atom. I have 3 shells, and my outermost shell holds 6 electrons." What is my atomic number?
column28: 3 shells means the first two are full: 2 + 8. Add the 6 in the third shell: 2 + 8 + 6 = 16 electrons. Neutral, so 16 protons: atomic number 16 (sulfur).
column29: If there are 3 shells, the inner two must be full. Add up all the electrons; neutral means e⁻ = p⁺.

column9: A neutral atom has the electron arrangement 2-8-8-1. The element with this atomic number has an average atomic mass of 39.098. How many neutrons are in an atom of its most common isotope?
column28: Electrons = 2 + 8 + 8 + 1 = 19, so p⁺ = 19 (potassium). Mass number = 39.098 rounded = 39. n⁰ = 39 − 19 = 20.
column29: Add the shells to get the electrons (= protons). Round the average atomic mass, then use mass number − atomic number.

column9: Maya drew a Bohr model of a neutral chlorine atom (atomic number 17): 2 electrons in the first shell, 8 in the second, and 8 in the third. What is wrong with her model?
column14: The third shell should have 7 electrons, because chlorine has only 17 electrons.
column15: The second shell can only hold 2 electrons.
column16: Chlorine needs a fourth shell for its last electron.
column17: Nothing is wrong; 2-8-8 is correct for chlorine.
column28: A neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons. 2 + 8 = 10, leaving 7 for the third shell: 2-8-7. Maya's 2-8-8 has 18 electrons, which is argon.
column29: Add up Maya's electrons. Does the total match the atomic number?

column9: Tungsten (W) has atomic number 74 and an average atomic mass of 183.84. In an atom of the most common isotope of tungsten, how many more neutrons are there than protons?
column28: Mass number = 183.84 rounded = 184. n⁰ = 184 − 74 = 110. Neutrons − protons = 110 − 74 = 36.
column29: Find the neutrons first (mass number − atomic number), then compare to the protons.

column9: A neutral atom has the electron arrangement 2-8-3 and has 14 neutrons. What is its mass number?
column28: Electrons = 2 + 8 + 3 = 13, so p⁺ = 13. Mass number = p⁺ + n⁰ = 13 + 14 = 27 (aluminum-27).
column29: Add the shells to get the electrons. Neutral means that is also the protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons.

column9: Put these atoms in order from FEWEST neutrons to MOST neutrons.
column28: Neutrons = mass # − atomic #: chlorine 35 − 17 = 18, calcium 40 − 20 = 20, argon 40 − 18 = 22, scandium 45 − 21 = 24. Ordering by atomic number or by mass number gives a different (wrong) order.
column29: Find the neutrons in each atom with mass number − atomic number, then sort.

column9: If two neutral atoms have the same mass number, they must be the same element.
column28: False. Only the number of protons (atomic number) identifies the element. Argon-40 (18 p⁺, 22 n⁰) and calcium-40 (20 p⁺, 20 n⁰) have the same mass number but are different elements.
column29: Mass number = protons + neutrons. Could two atoms reach the same total with different numbers of protons?

column9: All the protons in a nucleus are positive and packed very close together. Which statement best explains what this means for the nucleus?
column14: Opposite charges attract, so the protons pull each other in with no extra energy needed.
column15: Electrons sit inside the nucleus to cancel the protons' charge.
column16: Like charges repel, so an insane amount of energy is needed to hold the nucleus together.
column17: Protons lose their charge when they are inside the nucleus.
column28: Like charges repel, so the (+) protons push on each other, like springs squeezed into a box. An insane amount of energy holds the nucleus together. Electrons are in the electron cloud, not the nucleus.
column29: Do two positive charges attract or repel? What would it take to keep them squeezed together?

column9: Atom Q is neutral and has 2 shells with 1 electron in its outer shell. Atom R is neutral and has 7 more protons than atom Q. How many electrons are in the outermost shell of atom R?
column28: Q: 2 + 1 = 3 electrons, so 3 protons. R: 3 + 7 = 10 protons and 10 electrons. Fill 2-8, so the outermost shell has 8 electrons (neon).
column29: Find Q's atomic number from its shells, add 7 to get R's, then fill R's shells 2, 8, 8.
